sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We want the angle [MATH: \theta], as shown below. Note that the vector lies in the [MATH: 2]nd quadrant.

Applying the formula for the angle that a vector makes with the positive [MATH: x]-axis, we have the equation

[MATH: \tan θ|= (a_{y})/(a_{x}); = (3)/(− 2); = − (3)/(2).]

The solutions of this equation are

[MATH: θ|= \arctan (− (3)/(2)) + n ⋅ 180^{∘}; ≈ − 56.3^{∘} + n ⋅ 180^{∘},]

where [MATH: n] is any integer.

In this case, our vector is located in the [MATH: 2]nd quadrant, so we want a solution [MATH: 90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ.]

To get a solution in the desired range, we choose [MATH: n=1] and get

[MATH: θ|≈ − 56.3^{∘} + 180^{∘}; = 123.7^{∘}.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the smallest angle that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 2, -1 \rangle] makes with the positive [MATH: y]-axis. Round your answer to [MATH: 1] decimal place.
sections.readable_text: Find the smallest angle that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 2, -1 \rangle] makes with the positive [MATH: y]-axis. Round your answer to [MATH: 1] decimal place.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we need to find the angle [MATH: \theta] that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] makes with the positive [MATH: x]-axis. Applying the usual formula, we obtain the equation

[MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{a_y}{a_x} = \dfrac{-1}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}.]

The solutions of this equation are [MATH: θ|= \arctan (− (1)/(2)) + n ⋅ 180^{∘}; ≈ − 26.6^{∘} + n ⋅ 180^{∘},]

where [MATH: n] is any integer.

In this case, our vector is located in the [MATH: 4]th quadrant. Choosing [MATH: n=0], we get

[MATH: θ|≈ − 26.6^{∘}.]

Finally, to find the angle [MATH: \theta'] that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] makes with the positive [MATH: y]-axis, we add [MATH: 90^\circ] to the absolute value of the angle. This gives

[MATH: θ^{′}|=|θ|+ 90^{∘}; = 26.6^{∘} + 90^{∘}; = 116.6^{∘}.]

Item 2 — Tutorial: Finding the Angle Between a Vector in the First Quadrant and the Positive x-Axis

Content:
In general, for any vector [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \left< a_x, a_y \right>,] the angle [MATH: \theta] that the vector makes with the positive [MATH: x]-axis satisfies the equation
[MATH: \tan \theta = \dfrac{a_y}{a_x}.]

Content:
When the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] lies in the [MATH: 1]st quadrant, the desired solution to the above equation is just the principal value:
[MATH: \theta = \arctan\left(\dfrac{a_y}{a_x}\right)]

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Angle Between a Vector in the First Quadrant and the Positive x-Axis

Since the vector lies in the [MATH: 1]st quadrant, the desired solution to the above equation is just the principal value:

Content:
When the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] lies in a quadrant other than the [MATH: 1]st quadrant, we have to find a solution to the above equation that is in the desired range of values.

The general solution to the above equation is

Content:
where [MATH: n] is any integer.

- If [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is in the [MATH: 2]nd or [MATH: 3]rd quadrant, then the angle between [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and the positive [MATH: x]-axis is
[MATH: \theta = \arctan \left( \dfrac{a_y}{a_x} \right) + 180^\circ.]
- If [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is in the [MATH: 4]th quadrant, then the angle between [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and the positive [MATH: x]-axis is
[MATH: \theta = \arctan \left( \dfrac{a_y}{a_x} \right) + 360^\circ.]

where [MATH: n] is any integer.

In this case, our vector is located in the [MATH: 2]nd quadrant, so we want a solution [MATH: 90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ.]

To get a solution in the desired range, we choose [MATH: n=1] and get
